sentences.text: Dromaeosauroides bornholmensis is a genus within the family Dromaeosauridae.
Its name translates to 'Dromaeosaurus-like' and indicates its origin from the island of Bornholm.
The defining feature is a single tooth crown measuring 21.7 mm long, which is curved and finely serrated with six square denticles per millimeter.
Based on a tooth roughly 25% larger than Dromaeosaurus teeth, the animal's body length was estimated at 3 meters or more, possibly reaching 4 meters, with a total body weight of 40 kg.
This species holds the distinction of being the first and only scientifically named dinosaur known from Denmark.
It represents one of the earliest known dromaeosaurs and the first uncontested member of this group found in the Early Cretaceous of Europe.
The holotype tooth was officially certified as 'Danekræ', or the Danish creature, highlighting its scientific significance.
The genus was named by Christiansen and Bonde in 2003 after remains discovered in the Jydegaard Formation on the island of Bornholm.
The initial discovery occurred during a field course in September 2000 when a geology student named Eliza Jarl Estrup found the first dinosaur tooth on Danish territory.
A second tooth, measuring 15 mm in length with features identical to the holotype, was found later in 2008.
Studies suggest dromaeosaurs used their sickle claws to grasp prey while dismembering them with their mouths, similar to how modern birds of prey grip and pin down victims.
The development of deep snouts in dromaeosaurids was likely an adaptation for handling vertebrate prey.
Milàn and colleagues speculated that it could have used its enlarged sickle claw for 'spear fishing' to catch fish like Lepidotes, based on coprolite evidence.
Flight was considered unlikely for an animal of this size, despite some smaller dromaeosaurs potentially being capable of flight.

In 2003, Christiansen and Bonde classified it as a member of the Dromaeosaurinae subfamily within Dromaeosauridae due to similarities with Dromaeosaurus, though it is not part of that genus because the two lived 60 million years apart.
Dromaeosauroides lived during the Early Cretaceous period, specifically within the Berriasian age between 139.1 and 137.05 million years ago.
It inhabited a coastal lagoon environment alongside sauropods.
Remains of the Scandinavian-Russian Early Cretaceous fauna, including Dromaeosauroides, are found only in Bornholm and Scania.
In 2008, Johan Lindgren and colleagues considered it an indeterminate dromaeosaur.
In 2010, Oliver W. M. Rauhut and colleagues suggested that similar teeth might belong to the tyrannosauroid Proceratosaurus rather than Dromaeosauroides.
In 2021, Nicholas R. Longrich and colleagues proposed that it may have been an early eudromaeosaur.
